articles.title: Tafoya blames Kristi Noem, Minnesota leadership for ICE rollout
articles.summary: Minnesota Republican Senate candidate Michele Taforya on Sunday slammed her state’s leadership as well as former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem over the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) actions in the North Star State. “I’ve already said very publicly that I thought the ICE rollout here in Minnesota was very poorly handled, and Kristi Noem…
articles.body:
Minnesota Republican Senate candidate Michele Taforya on Sunday slammed her state’s leadership as well as former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem over the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) actions in the North Star State.

“I’ve already said very publicly that I thought the ICE rollout here in Minnesota was very poorly handled, and Kristi Noem was fired appropriately,” Tafoya told NewsNation’s Chris Stirewalt on “The Hill Sunday.”

“I’ll also give an F to the leadership here in Minnesota, however, for playing a part in that and not letting our local law enforcement help protect everyone. But I did think that was poorly handled, and I would say so,” she added.

In mid-February , White House border czar Tom Homan announced that Trump administration immigration crackdown efforts were set to end in Minnesota, following thousands of arrests and the January killings of two U.S. citizens, Alex Pretti and Renee Good, by federal agents.

The two deaths at the hands of federal immigration authorities in Minneapolis led to mass backlash against the Trump administration. Kristi Noem, the former Homeland Security secretary who was later replaced in her role, faced heat over the immigration efforts in the North Star State at the time.

The Republican Party more broadly has taken heat for its handling of immigration policy, according to fresh polling .

In a recent New York Times/Siena University poll, 52 percent of respondents backed Democrats’ performance on the issue of immigration over Republicans, while 45 percent backed Republicans over Democrats.

articles.title: Midterm history massively favors Democrats. But they are making a big mistake
articles.summary: Democrats need just five seats to flip the House, but their focus on subpoenas and lawsuits instead of affordability could undermine midterm hopes.
articles.body: Every two years, Washington performs the same ritual. The out-of-power party smells blood, the pundits write the eulogy early and by October the outcome seems like a foregone conclusion. But the history behind that confidence is more complicated than most imagine. What matters most in 2026 is not the electoral math — it’s what the party asking for power actually plans to do if they win. Over the last 80 years, the president's party has lost seats in the U.S. House of Representatives in 18 of 20 midterm elections. Political scientists call it the thermostat effect: Hand one party control of government, and the electorate instinctively seeks a counterweight, regardless of performance. Voter turnout compounds the challenge for the incumbent party. The winners tend to relax, while the losing side stays angry and shows up to the polls. Presidential elections offer a choice between two visions; midterms become a referendum on the party in charge. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: HOUSE CONTROL COULD HINGE ON WHETHER THE OLD POLITICAL RULES STILL APPLY This time, Republicans are also defending unusually narrow ground. Democrats only need a net gain of five seats to flip the majority. With approval ratings hovering below 45% for much of the year, the GOP finds itself squarely in the situation that historically produced the worst results for the president’s party. At the same time, our nation is grappling with a political moment with no clean precedent. Analysts keep applying old maps to new terrain. President Donald Trump is only the second president in American history to serve nonconsecutive terms. The other was President Grover Cleveland, who was elected in 1884, lost in 1888 and won again in 1892. VULNERABLE HOUSE REPUBLICANS EMBRACE TRUMP AS GOP BETS ON DEFYING MIDTERM HISTORY The fresh start with the electorate did little for Cleveland. By the time he reached the halfway point of his "second first term," voters handed his Democratic Party a major shellacking. Cleveland's Democrats lost roughly 116 House seats in 1894, amid a brutal depression. The outlook looks considerably more promising for Republicans. The electoral map underwent more changes in this election cycle than any in recent memory. Texas led the charge, redrawing its lines to the tune of five additional safe Republican seats. California countered with a map of its own, albeit favoring Democrats. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: DEMOCRATS LEAD IN THE HOUSE, BUT REDISTRICTING KEEPS THE GOP IN THE GAME The rest of the nation saw mixed results. Missouri, Ohio, North Carolina and Indiana moved right. Utah's court-ordered map favors Democrats. Virginia's attempted gerrymander was struck down entirely. The Supreme Court’s decision to leave both the Texas and California maps intact effectively canceled out the biggest moves on either side. The end result is a map that still tilts slightly Republican on net. Forecast models built on this terrain currently lean Democratic, but a lean is far from a lock. When voters head to the polls, they will reckon with one defining question: What are Democrats actually offering? On the trail, it is affordability, groceries, rent and healthcare, because it's real and it polls. But the gap between that message and the governing record is already visible where Democrats hold power. LIZ PEEK: DEMOCRATS’ AFFORDABILITY SCAM COLLAPSES IN STATES THEY ACTUALLY RUN Virginia Democrat Gov. Abigail Spanberger ran as the affordability governor after telling voters in writing she had no plans to redistrict the state, calling gerrymandering "detrimental to our democracy." She won, then backed the gerrymander anyway – the same one her own state Supreme Court struck down. She followed it with a ban on a wide range of semiautomatic rifles and magazines that two judges have since blocked. One found it likely unconstitutional and delayed implementation until 2027 at the earliest. Meanwhile, the Justice Department is suing to kill the measure permanently. None of that was a grocery bill. REDISTRICTING GIVES REPUBLICANS AN EDGE, BUT AFFORDABILITY WILL DECIDE THE MIDTERMS Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed built his Senate campaign on lowering healthcare costs through Medicare for All. Asked on "Meet the Press" whether people earning under $1 million would pay higher taxes under his plan, he didn't deny it. In fact, he called the trade-off "worth making." The end result is a map that still tilts slightly Republican on net. Forecast models built on this terrain currently lean Democratic, but a lean is far from a lock. Democrats are simply not focused on the kitchen table issues that win elections. Nationally, reporting from CNBC, Fox News and CNN over the past month confirms what House Democrats are actually planning if they take control of the House. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION It is not a comprehensive housing package or relief for hardworking Americans. Instead, they are building toward a sprawling investigative operation targeting President Trump, his Cabinet and his family. Subpoenas and lawsuits are already in motion before a single vote is cast. None of those actions will lower costs for anyone. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP History dictates this should be a good year for the party out of power. What history can't tell you is what a party does with power once it takes the reins. On that front, Democrats have already shown their hand. The American voter should take notice.

articles.title: Socialists are helping GOP campaigns heading into November
articles.summary: A Fox News poll finds 55% of voters view the Democratic Socialists of America unfavorably, fueling the GOP's midterm strategy against Democrats.
articles.body: A new number inside the latest Fox News national poll could bolster Republican midterm messaging as they work to hold their fragile congressional majorities amid an extremely rough political climate in this autumn's elections. The figure: 55% of registered voters hold an unfavorable view of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), while only three in 10 see the DSA in a positive light. The Fox News poll is the latest national survey to show that while the DSA has gained traction among Democrats, the group and the broader socialist movement in America face significant national skepticism. The figures appear to reinforce a key element in the GOP midterm playbook, which aims to turn what's normally a referendum on the party in power into a choice election. WHAT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POLL SAYS ABOUT THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS Republicans, pointing to the surge this year by progressive and socialist candidates over centrist and establishment-backed rivals in the Democratic Party primaries, are painting all Democrats on the ballot this year as far-left radicals. President Donald Trump, at this month's GOP midterm convention, argued that there is a "communist" takeover of the Democratic Party. "In state after state, the Democrat establishment has been overthrown and replaced by crazed lunatics and radicals. They call themselves Democrat socialists, but actually, they’re communists," Trump said. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB House Speaker Mike Johnson recently told Fox News Digital, "This really is a contrast election between common sense candidates... and crazy, and that's what the other side represents." Veteran Republican strategist Erin Maguire said that the new poll numbers on the DSA shows "that Democrats continuing to lurch further and further to the left with their socialist base is not something Americans want." "I do think it validates Republicans because Republicans are aiming to make this a choice election," Maguire, a veteran of the 2020 Trump re-election campaign who later steered communications for conservative firebrand Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, told Fox News Digital. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Democrats disagree and say the midterms will be won or lost over inflation. "Republicans are facing record-low approval numbers and have no midterm message after spiking costs, raising gas prices, and driving up inflation," Democratic National Committee Deputy Communications Director Kendall Witmer told Fox News Digital. But some moderate Democrats are concerned. "I think it’s a big problem," Ty Strong said as he referred to the Republican midterm strategy. Strong, founder and president of the Moderate PAC, told Fox News the midterms "should be a much bigger wave, but I don’t think it’s going to be as big as it could have been if we didn’t have this DSA and attacks that Republicans are going to use." WHO'S UP AND DOWN IN THE LATEST FOX NEWS MIDTERM ELECTION POWER RANKINGS He warned that the GOP playbook "absolutely could be effective." But Shannon Jackson, a key consultant and adviser to progressive leader Rep. Ro Khanna of California, said that "Republicans are in a very tough spot right now." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Referring to the Republican strategy, Jackson argued, "I think they’re reaching for things. I think the DSA issue is something they’re trying to make something, but it is not." "You can do these broad strokes of painting it as communist and things like that. They tried to do that for Bernie, and now he’s the most popular senator and politician in America," added Jackson, a grassroots organizer best known for his leadership roles in Sanders' 2016 and 2020 presidential campaigns.

articles.title: GOP takes aim at Congress' next 'get filthy rich' loophole after stock-trading ban
articles.summary: California Republican Young Kim targets earmark loopholes that let lawmakers indirectly enrich themselves and family members through federal spending.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: While the House successfully moved to rein in lawmakers' stock trading, a California Republican is targeting what she says is another avenue for congressional self-enrichment, citing members whose wealth has multiplied over the years. Rep. Young Kim's Stop Congressional Self-Enrichment Resolution comes after a successful GOP-led effort in July that imposed restrictions on stock purchases and requires several days' notice before stock sales. It also comes as Americans across the political spectrum remain frustrated by many lawmakers' rapidly growing wealth while in public office. "It could be earmarking a nonprofit organization where a member’s spouse sits on the board of directors or board of trustees, so it will indirectly benefit the family. Or it could earmark for a park at, let's say, an apartment building that a member or member's spouse or member’s children owns," Kim told Fox News Digital. SENATE QUIETLY BANS LAWMAKERS FROM BETTING ON PREDICTION MARKETS "And with the federal funds that the member brings and build the park nearby or community center nearby, it could increase the property value and therefore indirectly benefiting the member and their family members. Maybe asking to build a road up to rural land the member owns." Her new push would cover all material financial interests — direct or indirect — that benefit people beyond the lawmaker themselves. UNLIKELY BIPARTISAN SENATE DUO SEEKS TO PERMANENTLY BAN EX-LAWMAKERS FROM LOBBYING Current House rules require members requesting an earmark to certify that neither they nor their spouses have a financial interest in the recipient. Kim's bill would extend that requirement to immediate family members and indirect financial interests, such as nearby property values. "The days of members thinking that ‘I can use the community project funding request or bringing the earmarks for my district and get filthy rich off of it’— those days are numbered." WATCH: DEM CANDIDATE GRILLED ON STOCK TRADING AFTER BEING DUPED WITH SELFIE REQUEST "This is a good time because we see Americans are sick and tired of watching politicians getting filthy rich while average Americans are worrying about making ends meet and stretch every dollar that they earn." Citing the "Bridge to Nowhere" project in Alaska's Inside Passage in the early 2000s as a symbol of concerns over earmarks, Kim said the ensuing decade-long moratorium curbed abuse. Kim said safeguards put in place after the moratorium have helped, but argued members are still able to provide themselves with indirect benefits. She reiterated that she is not targeting any individuals. While there are now apps out there like the "Pelosi Stock Tracker" and others that let retail investors see which stocks are being bought or sold by which members, Kim said her effort does not target any one colleague. 'SQUAD' DEM DISMISSES FRAUD PROBE SPECULATION AFTER $29M NET-WORTH DROP "And, this is not in any way discouraging members to fight for their districts and bring in the appropriate taxpayer dollars for projects near their districts," she said. "That is so important," she said, pointing to funding she brought to Orange County to prevent and recover from recent wildfires, among other interests for her constituents. "That's what we are sent to do, fight for our district, but not at the expense of, you know, enriching. I mean, not at the expense of hurting our very constituents that we are trying to support while we are lining our pockets, because there are too many career politicians in Washington looking out for no one but themselves." Innumerable lawmakers have come under fire over the decades for their earmarking prowess. In one notable case, then-House Speaker Dennis Hastert, R-Ill., faced criticism in 2006 over a $207 million earmark to build a parkway near property he owned. Amid the kerfuffle, an attorney for the leader pushed back on what he called a "libelous" allegation from a good-government group about it at the time. The attorney said criticizing Hastert for the project was akin to "complaining about a purchase in Alexandria based on renovations at the Capitol." GOP LAWMAKER UNDER HOUSE ETHICS REVIEW BLASTS 'BASELESS' INVESTIGATION In 2023, the Boston Globe reported that earmarks secured by Rep. Stephen Lynch, D-Mass., benefited a health center in Boston where his wife was employed. Two million dollars went to the South Boston Community Health Center, and another $1 million went to a foundation where Lynch’s wife was an unpaid director. Fox News Digital reached out to Lynch for comment. Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., previously secured earmarks totaling $3.5 million for George Mason University, where his wife had served as interim president and later as a professor. The earmarks "are in no way influenced by Secretary Holton," a Kaine spokesperson told The Messenger news outlet at the time — referencing former Virginia Education Secretary Anne Holton. "Secretary Holton has no involvement in the [Congressionally Directed Spending] CDS process, and no involvement in the George Mason CDS requests," the spokesperson added. "Senator Kaine and Secretary Holton have not discussed the requests." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER With the Senate next to take up stock trading prohibitions, Kim’s bill stands as a gap closer, she said, on a practice that has rare emphatic bipartisan support. articles.title: Elon Musk is flying under the radar in the Texas Senate race. Republicans want to keep it that way.
articles.summary: The last time Elon Musk sank money into an election, he played a starring role in the 2025 state Supreme Court race in Wisconsin.
articles.body: The last time Elon Musk sank money into an election, he played a starring role in the 2025 state Supreme Court race in Wisconsin. He donned an oversized cheese hat, offered $1 million checks to voters, and he and affiliated groups poured at least $20 million into the contest. In the end, the conservative candidate lost by 10 points in what was widely viewed as a rebuke of Musk and the Trump administration. Now, the richest person in the world is back boosting Republican candidates in critical midterm elections, including a bruising Senate race in Texas where Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton is facing Democrat James Talarico, who had initially far outraised him and remains close in polling. But that financial tide is quickly turning — with Musk’s help. Unlike in Wisconsin, Musk has so far stayed out of the spotlight in Texas, even though he lives in the state, has based his companies Tesla and SpaceX there, and employs about 20,000 people. He hasn’t announced plans for any in-person events, or teased — as he did in Wisconsin — that he’d be handing out $1 million checks to voters. Privately, Republicans say they want Musk to keep his distance. In interviews, more than half a dozen Republican strategists involved in the Texas Senate race say they hope Musk follows his 2024 model of electoral involvement, which led to a Republican sweep of the White House and Congress. Then, Musk spent more than $250 million on Donald Trump and his party. Republicans believe Democrats will attempt to turn Musk into a boogeyman if he takes on a higher-profile role in Texas or other battlegrounds. One Republican consultant involved in the Texas Senate race said that was the perception in Wisconsin. “He came in super late, and it was very public,” said the consultant, who, like others interviewed for this article, were granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Elon spending money became the story, which I think maybe was a mistake.” A different Republican strategist involved in Texas campaigns said those around Musk learned from the experience. “Did Elon bring some things to the Wisconsin race that hampered things? Probably,” the person added. “But I think they will adjust for that.” Democrats, however, say they welcome Musk more publicly entering the fray in Texas. “Elon, bring it. You’ve failed in Wisconsin. You’ll fail in Texas,” said Nathan Johnson, a Democrat running to replace Paxton as attorney general. “I’m not afraid of Elon bringing his political money here. All these policies favor him or people like him.” An in-your-face Musk campaign would play into Talarico’s narrative that the real American divide isn’t left versus right but “top versus bottom,” with elites and billionaires exerting control over the working class, they say. “James is running largely on costs and corruption,” Luke Warford, a Texas-based Democratic strategist and chair of the Travis County Democratic Party, said of Talarico. “The idea of the richest man in the world coming in late to try to buy the election and save Ken Paxton really plays into James Talarico’s argument.” The Texas Senate race has all the makings of a contest that would attract Musk. The conservative narrative building against Talarico amplifies his past remarks in support of transgender people, including his comment that “God is nonbinary.” Talarico told Fox News he was being “provocative” and was trying to convey that one cannot use “human categories to define God.” Musk has spoken publicly about his own transgender daughter, Vivian Jenna Wilson, saying she was “not a girl” and was figuratively “dead.” He also alleged that he had been “tricked” into authorizing trans-related medical treatment for her when she was 16. Wilson previously told NBC News that Musk was an absent father who was cruel to her as a child for being queer and feminine. At this point, Musk’s America PAC has not said how much it will invest in Texas, but a person with knowledge of the group’s thinking indicated that as of now, the Paxton-Talarico contest was not slotted to receive more focus than other Senate or congressional races the group is investing in across the country, saying “every state and district where we are spending is a priority.” To date, America PAC has spent nearly $5.2 million on digital ads, mail, live calls and pamphleting in Texas, but that number is expected to significantly climb. In all, the super PAC has spent $14.7 million on congressional races, including seven Senate races and nearly three dozen House races. The group has spent the most money on the Texas Senate race, followed by nearly $3 million on Senate races in Ohio and Michigan. National Republican groups long knew they would have to provide air cover for Paxton because of an initial fundraising disadvantage to Talarico, who had $21 million in cash on hand compared to Paxton’s $1.7 million at the end of June, according to campaign finance reports. Today, a flood of Republican money is pouring in from several sources and the balance has suddenly tipped in Paxton’s favor. “America PAC is working in full coordination with the entire GOP apparatus and is investing in the states and districts that will decide control of the House and Senate,” America PAC spokesman Andrew Romeo said in a statement. “Our only priority is ensuring Republicans keep full control of Washington and stopping the lunatic left from bringing us back to the days of open borders, rampant crime, and woke policies.” Paxton’s status as a scandal-plagued candidate who has been impeached and indicted — coupled with the fact he’s coming off a contentious primary against Sen. John Cornyn and much of the Republican Party establishment, aside from Trump — makes him among the most vulnerable front-line Senate Republican candidates in a state where Democrats have not won a statewide post in three decades. After Trump’s late endorsement helped propel Paxton over Cornyn, groups like the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, were left scrambling. The election cycle budgets were, in part, built on the idea that Cornyn would not need nearly as much national fundraising help. “Cornyn had his own fundraising machine, he could raise a lot of money on his own, so it was going to make things easier to cover other important close races,” said a Republican consultant familiar with the thought process. “I know they [Elon] are focused more on the ground game stuff. MAGA Inc. is on digital and mail. This pretty much turned out the way we thought it would. It’s an expensive endeavor and a team and multigroup effort.” The pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC has pumped at least $15 million into TV ads that have included hitting Talarico on previous votes involving China. So far, MAGA Inc. has spent $10 million in the state to help boost Paxton, its second-biggest single-state investment. The group did not return a request for comment, but in an interview with NBC News last week, MAGA Inc. chief James Blair said the group had booked $10 million worth of TV ad time in Texas. Blair noted the previous disparity in spending, with Talarico and related groups pummeling Paxton on TV. “The fact is Ken Paxton had $100 million spent against him in the primary,” Blair said. “Talarico had $0 spent against him in the primary, and that has an impact on candidate images that takes time to rectify. But the resources … have begun to be deployed now in earnest [and] will take care of that problem.” A veteran GOP official directly involved in the race contended that the shift toward spending in Texas did not take away from other battlegrounds. “This spending will not take away from other investments,” the official said. “This came from a collection of Texas folks very committed to making sure that seat remains Republican. They see the polling, and that James Talarico is so extreme. No one wants to see Texas turn blue.” When asked about the onslaught of money headed toward Talarico, spokesman JT Ennis said, “Billionaire-backed dark money groups are lying about James because they’re scared of the people-powered movement we’re building to fix this broken, corrupt political system.”

articles.title: DC Courts pleads with Congress for funding as system reaches tipping point
articles.summary: Years of flat funding are stretching the District of Columbia Courts thin, placing a system relied on by thousands each day under what officials describe as unsustainable pressure. It’s left administrators, judges and clerks to juggle an ever-growing caseload and heightened security needs with a budget that hasn’t kept pace. “We have certainly reached a critical inflection point,” said…
articles.body:
Years of flat funding are stretching the District of Columbia Courts thin, placing a system relied on by thousands each day under what officials describe as unsustainable pressure.

It’s left administrators, judges and clerks to juggle an ever-growing caseload and heightened security needs with a budget that hasn’t kept pace.

“We have certainly reached a critical inflection point,” said Herbert Rouson Jr., the executive officer of D.C. Courts.

And the system is unique in that it is entirely federally funded.

D.C. Courts, which includes both the trial and appeals courts for the nation’s capital, is requesting $298.1 million from Congress for the next fiscal year — a $35 million increase to its operating budget to address the caseload, strengthen cyber and physical security, and maintain essential services.

“Funding levels have remained unchanged since fiscal year 2023, but the demand for court services has actually surged since that time,” Rouson said.

The strain, he said, can be felt in the courts’ workload.

Filings across both D.C. Superior Court and the D.C. Court of Appeals have been on the rise since 2023, with the number of criminal cases up by 150 percent and domestic violence misdemeanors up by roughly 37 percent.

And because the courts generally function similarly to a state court, the system doesn’t get to decide which cases it hears.

“Every case that’s filed, we have to do something with it,” Rouson said. “We have to handle it. We have to process it, and that takes staff to do.”

That often means also handling cases brought by federal prosecutors in the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, which acts as the local district attorney for most felony offenses committed by adults within the district.

Inside one nearly full Superior Court courtroom, a judge apologized for the proceedings being delayed but said some attorneys had yet to check in. On her calendar were more than a dozen criminal case hearings — ranging from misdemeanors to a theft on the Metro to a National Guardsman accused of pointing a gun at a fellow Guard member during an argument.

The court’s docket was so full that one attorney assured a client that he would be back, saying he was needed in three different courtrooms that morning.

Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, Rouson said roughly 10,000 people would walk through the courthouse doors on any given day. He suspects that number is “creeping back up,” especially as U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro leads an aggressive local crime crackdown at President Trump’s direction.

The prosecutorial shift, which began to take hold last August, has resulted in more individuals passing through arraignment court. The “no paper” rate — the percentage of arrests made by D.C. police where prosecutors choose not to file charges — has dropped below 5 percent, according to officials.

Early warning signs of a system in distress are also reflected in a criminal clearance rate that has fallen from 108 percent to 60 percent in just three fiscal years, meaning cases are being filed faster than the courts can resolve them.

Congress has provided some help, recently confirming eight judges to fill vacancies on the bench. But officials said more judges alone can’t offset the backlog.

“Those efforts are welcome,” Anna Blackburne-Rigsby, chief judge of the D.C. Court of Appeals, and Milton Lee Jr., chief judge of the D.C. Superior Court, wrote in an August op-ed for The Washington Post . “But adding judges without providing the workforce and infrastructure to support them limits the efficacy of that investment. Justice depends on an entire system working together.”

It isn’t just a matter of personnel, either. Wrapped into the D.C. Courts’ budget request is an additional $10 million for physical and cybersecurity that officials say is needed to thwart attempted online attacks and protect judges.

That is not an unfamiliar appeal to lawmakers. When Supreme Court Justice Amy Coney Barrett appeared before Congress in July alongside Justice Elena Kagan, she testified that there was a “really high” threat level facing federal judges.

And that doesn’t just apply to the federal bench. Rouson said there have been approximately 800 investigations of threats against D.C. Courts judges, which has raised the demand for better courthouse security.

Yet House appropriators have approved a budget that would see funding for D.C. Courts cut by $18 million in fiscal 2027, a figure that officials say is roughly equivalent to the Courts’ entire annual security costs or the cost of processing 3,600 criminal cases.

The budget proposal has yet to make it to the full House floor for a vote. And the Senate version of the appropriations bill is still pending in committee.

“That would just force us to choose between some critical security investments and compromising our court operations and the delivery of service that really the public has come to expect of this court, and that we feel the public is really due,” Rouson said.

He said the D.C. Courts have already taken steps over the past four years to cut costs to avoid falling into a deficit, scaling back on hiring, contracts and other various expenses. Certain maintenance projects have also been put off.

“There’s really no more meat on those bones,” he added, suggesting the repeated years of flat funding have created an untenable situation.

About three-quarters of the budget goes toward personnel services, while the balance covers other matters, such as janitorial and security contracts.

“You’re not gonna cut there, right?” That makes matters worse,” Rouson said. He noted that having to turn staffing reductions would only further exacerbate problems by creating greater delays in case processing.

Unlike other jurisdictions where local governments are responsible for setting funding levels, the district’s mayor and council have no say in the matter.

“D.C. doesn’t have the ability for local politicians to assess what’s causing caseload increase and make a political decision locally,” Thomas said. “This is just another one of those clear products of complicated home rule that do make this different because there are fewer levers of decision making about our courts and how they function.”

A group of more than 300 D.C. businesses, organizations and individuals hand delivered a letter to lawmakers on the Senate Appropriations Committee on Thursday, urging them to fully fund the court system.

“Efficiency matters, but there is a floor: When limited capacity leads to delays or errors, confidence in the process rightfully erodes,” said Bridgette Stumpf, the executive director and co-founder of Volare, which provides crime victims in the district with free legal services.

“And those failures are not cost-neutral — they carry a financial cost to the system and a far heavier human cost for the people waiting on it to deliver justice.”

articles.title: College sports bill faces uphill battle in post-midterms House
articles.summary: Bipartisan legislation to regulate the growing business behind college sports appears primed to clear the Senate this week, but it faces a much tougher road in the House when lawmakers return in the fall. The Protect College Sports Act, championed by Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), cleared its first major congressional tests…
articles.body:
Bipartisan legislation to regulate the growing business behind college sports appears primed to clear the Senate this week, but it faces a much tougher road in the House when lawmakers return in the fall.

The Protect College Sports Act, championed by Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), cleared its first major congressional tests last week, winning the backing of more than 70 senators on two procedural votes, including a group of key Democrats and conservatives who had held out support for weeks.

Cruz had insisted a big bipartisan vote was key to gaining enough momentum to win over skeptical House members, and in private conversations, he urged Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to keep members in town last week to take up his bill.

But Johnson decided to send House members home early, meaning the legislation will not reach President Trump’s desk until November at the earliest.

“We remain pretty optimistic the House is going to make this a priority when they come back. The only reason you wouldn’t do that is because of sour grapes,” said one lobbyist who has worked extensively on the Senate bill. “They owe it to the American people, and especially for Republicans, to the expectations of the president on top of that.”

Trump endorsed the act and last week called out a pair of GOP senators from Florida who joined Democrats in voting against the measure over its provisions relating to conference realignment.

The legislation would grant student athletes a new federal right to earn compensation for their name, image and likeness. It caps agent fees at 5 percent, guarantees scholarships for 10 years after eligibility and allows athletes to transfer once without having to sit out a year.

The bill would also prevent coaches from leaving midseason to coach or otherwise effectively take over another program during the same competitive season, a major point of contention this fall in the wake of Louisiana State University football coach Lane Kiffin’s departure from Ole Miss last year.

Critics of the bill call it a gift to the NCAA and top conferences, which they argue would more easily be able to stifle the earning potential of athletes and protect wealthy coaches and administrators.

“The Protect College Sports Act sells out athletes and bails out the NCAA,” said Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), one of the bill’s most vocal critics and a lawmaker who played football at Stanford University.

“If this bill becomes law, the same actors who exploited college athletes for decades will emerge with more power, and college athletes will emerge with less,” he said.

The act’s recent progress is the closest the NCAA has come to gaining the congressional antitrust protection it has been seeking for months, a prerogative it has spent tens of millions of dollars chasing.

The organization has cut ads with legendary football coach Nick Saban urging the bill’s passage and organized meetings between top coaches and skeptical lawmakers as amendments to the bill were being finalized.

The coach meetings included John Calipari, who after stops at the universities of Massachusetts and Kentucky is the University of Arkansas men’s basketball coach; Mark Few, the basketball coach at Gonzaga University; and University of Houston basketball coach Kelvin Sampson.

“It’s not perfect, but I believe this will solve 75 to 80 percent of our issues, and it’s been special to see both parties come together on this,” Calipari said in a video posted to social media after he returned from Capitol Hill.

If the Protect College Sports Act is to succeed, its backers will need to win the support of lawmakers who killed the SCORE Act, a similar bill that died in the House after the Congressional Black Caucus (CBC) and NAACP came out against it.

Labor groups and the CBC argue antitrust protection for the NCAA and member conferences would disproportionately limit the earning potential of minority student athletes, particularly in Southern states with powerhouse football and basketball teams.

“I was totally against the SCORE Act; I haven’t read this one, but we’ll see,” Rep. James Clyburn (D-S.C.) told the Hill. “If they’ve not done better on that [antitrust] subject and a couple of others, then I’m going to be against it. But I’ll be working with the Congressional Black Caucus on it.”

Some Republicans in the lower chamber who opposed the SCORE Act — which stands for Student Compensation and Opportunity through Rights and Endorsements — also expressed hesitation and argued lawmakers have more important priorities.

“Ted’s got some good things in the bill and I’ve got some things that are concerning. We’ve got to do something, but it has to be sufficient enough,” Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) told The Hill. “But right now, the last thing we need to do is campaign on sports when we need to do the SAVE [American] Act and cut spending.”

The Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act is controversial election legislation backed by Trump and much of the GOP.

Others in the lower chamber predict a change to the system governing college athletics is inevitable, even if disagreements on how to rectify the issues facing the NCAA persist.

“College sports has been really hurt by the current system, but what I don’t want to do is put in place a permanent system that makes it worse,” Rep. Bryan Steil (R-Wis.) told The Hill. “It unquestionably affects not only a lot of Americans but a lot of students. Everybody agrees the current system is failing, but getting it right is going to be the essential piece.”

Washington Capitals winger Alex Ovechkin broke his silence on an ad he appeared in last week promoting Russian President Vladimir Putin that sparked international backlash ahead of what could be the future Hall of Famer’s final season in the NHL. “I’m Russian, I’m going to live there when I’m done. My kids [are] going to be there. My family’s going to be there, you know, I support my country. That’s it,” Ovechkin said, clarifying he is not “pro-war” and hopes to see “peace and love” overseas as Putin continues to wage war on Ukraine.

The National Park Service has secretly awarded contracts to development firms in connection with the administration’s plans for East Potomac Park, the site of East Potomac Golf Links. Democrats on the House Natural Resources Committee blasted the administration for moving forward with the project despite a lawsuit seeking to stop it, warning Trump is “systematically moving to take this historic, publicly accessible resource and turn it into another gilded private golf club for the mega-rich.”

University of Texas quarterback Arch Manning apologized after he laughed in front of reporters talking about an AI-generated video depicting his coach slapping a female ESPN reporter. Manning in a statement posted to his Instagram account said “it’s easy to say I didn’t mean it, but I know my words and actions were hurtful to a lot of people. I do not take that lightly and am deeply sorry for that.” The Longhorns are the top-ranked team in the country, and sportsbooks have Manning listed as one of the favorites to win the Heisman Trophy this year.

Jocks on the Hill: Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-Md.)

Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-Md.), who served as the state’s attorney in Prince George’s County, answered some sports questions for The Hill.

“Basketball, I’ve always been deep into it. I was waiting for that growth spurt to happen, and it never happened.”

“This will show you how old I am, I used to pull for the Knicks when I was a kid because the Bullets hadn’t moved to D.C. yet. I’ve been a Wizards fan, but with the Knicks, old habits die hard.”

Is there an athlete you admired growing up?

“I liked Walt Frazier … and Dr. J [Julius Erving] and Bill Bradley were probably the reason I decided I wanted to go to Princeton.”

Hate is a strong word, but is there a team you love to root against?

“Duke men’s basketball and the Dallas Cowboys. That one was easy. They did a 30 for 30 on Christian Laettner … his sister was getting death threats? I was like whoa … that’s a little much.”

Why do you think sports bring people together in politically divided times?

“Sports brings people together in all times, and I really think we need it now more than ever.”

With all the chatter about huge sums of money flooding into college sports, The Wall Street Journal published a timely scoop revealing Jolin Ellison, the wife of billionaire Larry Ellison, as one of the University of Michigan’s top boosters who has poured millions into the school’s athletic department.

The Athletic has a deep dive into the Arizona State University men’s hockey program, which sparked a firestorm this summer after a player collapsed during an intense workout, an incident that has raised questions about training methods at the school.

The Ringer’s Lindsay Jones asks a pointed question in her latest piece for the outlet. She’s one of a growing number of people who follow college football and are asking: “How many times can we declare the Bill Belichick College Football Experience to be a flop?

articles.title: Texas poll: James Talarico holds a narrow advantage for Senate while Greg Abbott leads for governor
articles.summary: Democrat James Talarico holds a narrow advantage over Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race, but within the margin of error, according to a new poll, while Republican Gov.
articles.body: Democrat James Talarico holds a narrow advantage over Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race, but within the margin of error, according to a new poll, while Republican Gov. Greg Abbott holds a wider lead over Democrat Gina Hinojosa in the contest for governor, as economic issues and immigration drive voter decision-making. The new NBC5 Dallas/Telemundo Station Group poll shows Talarico at 46% and Paxton at 43%, within the survey’s margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. Another 8% of potential voters were still up for grabs in the race — just as tens of millions of dollars in advertising from Republican groups began to flood into the state. Abbott took 48% to Hinojosa’s 41% in the gubernatorial race, a broader edge that’s also technically within the margin of error. The survey effort also zeroed in on Latinos in Texas, shows how that group of voters has swung back to the left since President Donald Trump won 55% of the Hispanic vote in Texas in 2024, according to NBC News exit polling. Both Talarico and Hinojosa led with Latinos by double digits, with Talarico up 18 points (54%-36%) and Hinojosa up 13 points (52%-39%). But that may still fall short of the benchmark the candidates would need to pull out a victory in a state that hasn’t elected a statewide Democrat in three decades. At a UnidosUS conference in August, Hinojosa indicated a previous Democratic marker at 64% would be enough to win. “To give you a sense of our importance in this election, in 2018, the closest a Democrat came to flipping Texas in recent history, Beto O’Rourke ran against Ted Cruz and he got 64% of the Latino vote,” Hinojosa said then. “When I get 64% of the Latino vote in 2026, I win.” Hispanic voters hold enormous electoral power in Texas, making up about a third of the state’s electorate. The survey included 401 Hispanic likely voters in Texas, who were interviewed live by telephone by Mason-Dixon Polling & Research, Inc. from Sept. 8-12. The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 5 points. The same firm conducted the broader survey of 625 likely voters in Texas Sept. 8-10. In both surveys, economic factors ranked the highest when it came to voter motivations, with immigration issues ranking the second-highest for Hispanic voters. Among all voters, the top issues identified were the economy and jobs at 24%, inflation and the cost of living at 23%, immigration and the border at 18%, and healthcare at 10%. Among Hispanic voters, inflation and the cost of living topped their concerns, with 33% saying it had the greatest influence on their vote. The next highest concern was immigration and the border at 23%, followed by the economy and jobs at 19%, and healthcare at 9%. Crime and public safety, education and housing all ranked in the single digits. Overall, Texas voters lined up strongly in favor of restrictions on gender transition-related medical treatments for minors, with 63% supporting and 29% opposing restrictions. On a related question, 61% of respondents believed students should only use the bathroom for the sex they were assigned at birth and 8% saying students should be allowed to use the bathroom for the gender with which they identify. Most of the remainder said schools should provide gender-neutral bathrooms. Notably, however, social issues such as abortion and trans rights ranked low on the list of issues that voters said would influence their candidate choices. Overall, abortion and trans rights ranked at 6% importance among all groups and at 4% among Hispanic voters. That low mark is significant, as Republican super PACs have already spent millions of dollars on TV and digital ads, particularly targeting Talarico, with messaging squarely focused on trans issues. Voters statewide were more or less split on whether Texas should cooperate with ICE on vehicle pursuits and traffic stops. While Hispanic voters were about evenly split on the question — 45% saying Texas should cooperate, 48% saying it shouldn’t –– white voters were far more favorable toward cooperation: 62% in support of cooperation, 32% against it. It was the reverse for Black voters. Of those surveyed, 66% of Black voters say the state should not cooperate with ICE on the stops and 24% said it should. Immigration questions broke sharply along ideological lines. In the survey of all Texas voters, 93% of Republicans said local police officers should be allowed to question individuals about their immigration status during lawful encounters, while 11% of Democrats and 50% of independents supported the policy. The surveys explored other areas, including a question on a voucher program that’s been controversial in the state. Sixty-three percent of those queried said they opposed allowing state tax dollars to be used to pay for private school tuition, with 30% supporting it and another 7% undecided statewide.

articles.title: Senate GOP sees battleground map widen amid voter anger over economy
articles.summary: Senators in both parties say the Senate midterm election battleground map has expanded significantly six weeks before Election Day, putting the GOP majority in greater jeopardy. Several solidly Republican-leaning states — including Kansas and Nebraska — are now seen as being in play, the senators say. Democrats can also add New Hampshire to the list…
articles.body:
Senators in both parties say the Senate midterm election battleground map has expanded significantly six weeks before Election Day, putting the GOP majority in greater jeopardy.

Several solidly Republican-leaning states — including Kansas and Nebraska — are now seen as being in play, the senators say.

Democrats can also add New Hampshire to the list of toss-up seats they are defending. The Granite State and Michigan are hosting competitive races that are providing hope for Republicans and some nervousness for Democrats.

But overall, the widening map is putting more pressure on Republicans.

While Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) is seen as relatively safe in Georgia, a number of GOP incumbents are looking nervously at polls given the changing dynamics.

The senators point to voter anger over rising gas and diesel prices as the biggest factor driving the shift of sentiment toward Democrats even in traditionally GOP-leaning states.

“Donald Trump is doing everything he can to sabotage the campaigns of Republican incumbents,” said Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.). “This could be a big blue wave, absolutely.”

Democratic senators want to see their leaders get aggressive by pouring money into GOP states as polls show Democratic candidates could win in places that were thought to be out of reach only a few months ago.

“I think we have nine Senate pickups possible and need to put our resources into making sure we win as many of those that we can,” Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) said.

Senators in both parties say Democratic candidates have growing momentum because of rising energy prices. Voters are blaming the increasing costs on the military conflict with Iran, which President Trump started back in February without prior authorization from Congress.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) told The Hill that Democrats are expanding the Senate map “big time.”

Polls show close Senate races in Maine, Ohio, Iowa, Texas and Alaska, and the Democratic candidate pulling away in North Carolina.

One GOP senator said internal polls show the Kansas and Nebraska Senate races are very close and the “overall environment” is bad for Republicans.

“Energy prices are way too high. The war, people don’t like. And the real reason they don’t like the war is it’s making everything more expensive. Voters are not in a good mood. In farm states like Nebraska and Kansas, farmers are just irate about the beef issue, they’re irate about energy prices,” the senator said. “It’s a tough environment.”

To be sure, the GOP remains a heavy favorite in both Nebraska and Kansas.

Kansas and Nebraska are both seen as likely GOP seats by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report. Florida and South Carolina are among the states where the GOP is seeking to retain seats that Cook rates as solidly Republican.

Still, the senator who spoke to The Hill called recent polls showing rising voter anger over gas prices and the war in Iran “grim” for the GOP and underscore worries about a widening map.

A Fox News poll of 1,211 registered voters nationwide conducted from Sept. 11-14 found that 71 percent of Americans said the Trump administration lacks a plan to end the Iran war and 34 percent of voters rated the cost of living and inflation as the top issue in this year’s election — more important than any other issue.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) said the Iran war’s impact on diesel and gas prices has become a major political problem.

“This is what people are talking about. How do we address it? I think we have to recognize, yes, we have seen the prices of fuel and related products, diesel — other refined products, fertilizer, we have seen all that rise as a consequence of what we’re seeing in Iran,” she said.

“People are feeling it, and they don’t like it. They don’t like it at all. And what kind of response are we seeing from the White House? Is there a recognition that there’s a connection here? If there is, I’m not hearing anybody enunciate it,” she added, expressing frustration over the president’s response to high energy prices.

Senate Republicans acknowledge they now face tough Senate races in several Midwestern states because farmers are angry over the cost of fuel and the impact of Trump’s trade policies, especially a recent decision by the president to allow 300,000 metric tons of foreign beef imports into the United States.

“Clearly beef is a critical issue for us. Our producers love the president, they consider him to be one of their own, and what he did in sending a message about increasing beef supplies in the United States by bringing in outside [foreign] beef really hurt them,” said Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), whose reelection race is rated solid Republican by Cook.

“That has shown up in his ratings in places that normally would be solidly in his corner. They’re frustrated and they’re hurt,” he said of the backlash among farmers against Trump.

Rounds said that’s “absolutely” giving Democrats a chance to win in Kansas and Nebraska, where the local economies depend heavily on farming.

A new Hill/Emerson College Polling survey conducted among 750 likely voters in Kansas from Sept. 15-16 showed Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton leading incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall, 45 percent to 43 percent.

A Republican source familiar with the race said private polling also showed Hamilton with a slight lead.

Some polls showed a tight race in Nebraska, where independent candidate Dan Osborn is within a few points of incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts (R).

A Wedgewood Polls survey of 500 likely voters conducted from Sept. 14-16 showed Ricketts ahead by 4 points while a SurveyUSA poll of 503 likely voters conducted from Sept. 8-13 showed Osborn with a 4-point lead.

Ricketts did not dispute that Nebraska is now in play in the battle for the Senate majority.

“I’ve been taking my race seriously for over a year,” he said when asked about Democratic claims that the battleground map has expanded to the Cornhusker State.

Democrats are growing more confident, with some pointing to a InsiderAdvantage poll of 1,200 likely voters conducted from Sept. 8-9 to say their party could win South Carolina. The poll showed that Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) is only 2 points ahead of her Democratic opponent, pediatrician Annie Andrews.

“I just saw Annie Andrews yesterday, I believe she has a real shot at this,” Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) told The Hill. He said he plans to campaign for Andrews.

“She’d be great to have in our caucus. We don’t have a physician on our side of the aisle. … I’d love to see her win,” Kelly said.

Republicans argued they’ve expanded the map to put Michigan and Minnesota — two Democratic-leaning seats — within their reach, as well as the race for the seat being vacated by the retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.).

Cook rates New Hampshire and Michigan as toss-ups, while Minnesota is likely Democratic.

But Real Clear Politics, the nonpartisan media company that tracks polls and elections, on Friday moved the Minnesota Senate race to “toss-up” status.

Bernadette Breslin, a spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee, said Democrats are talking about Republican-leaning states such as Kansas, Nebraska and South Carolina being in play to distract from Republican threats in Democratic-leaning states such as New Hampshire and Minnesota.

“Chuck Schumer’s claim that the Senate map is expanding for Democrats is false spin meant to distract from his waning hopes of rescuing [New Hampshire’s Democratic Senate nominee] Chris Pappas and [Minnesota’s Democratic Senate nominee] Peggy Flanagan in states he once thought were safe,” Breslin said.

A KSTP/SurveyUSA poll of 654 likely voters in Minnesota conducted from Sept. 9-14 showed Flanagan tied with Republican Michele Tafoya, 42 percent to 42 percent.

Marshall says he feels good about his race, but he warned that affordability is a major issue and that it will be critical that low-propensity voters who support Trump show up to the polls on Election Day.

Kansas hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.

articles.title: House GOP not done with ActBlue after bombshell internal memos raise foreign cash questions
articles.summary: House GOP investigators warn their ActBlue probe is far from over as new findings allege the platform green-lighted donations despite foreign red flags.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: House GOP investigators are warning that they are not done with ActBlue after a bombshell report fueled questions over whether the Democrat fundraising giant is accepting foreign cash and lying to Congress about it. "Whether it’s allowing fraudsters to steal taxpayer dollars or accepting illegal foreign donations through ActBlue, Democrats have proven themselves to be the party of fraud. Our investigation into ActBlue is far from over. We expect more documents and testimony in the weeks ahead," House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., told Fox News Digital. ActBlue is a massive platform for campaigns to raise money that's used by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and the Democratic leaders of the House and Senate, among others. Republican lawmakers have long accused the company of having lax verification standards for donors, something ActBlue has said it actively improved since the start of the GOP's probe. But new findings, first reported by Fox News Digital, appear to show employees green-lighting donations despite some questions about where they came from. FAR-LEFT POLITICIANS STILL USING ACTBLUE AS 88-YEAR-OLD DISPUTES DONATING NEARLY $150,000 TO FUNDRAISING GIANT But the company maintains it did nothing wrong and signaled in comments to Fox News Digital that it has no plans to return any donations raised in the report. HOUSE DEM LASHES OUT AT GOP EFFORTS TO PROBE FOREIGN DONATIONS WITH STUNNING CLAIM ON MOTIVE Committee on House Administration Chairman Bryan Steil, R-Wis., told Fox News Digital on Friday, "ActBlue’s own admissions raise serious questions about its fraud prevention practices, including a so-called passport verification process that did not actually verify or check entries against any government database. All options are on the table to ensure we get to the bottom of what is going on at ActBlue." And a spokesperson for Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, and the House Judiciary Committee confirmed to Fox News Digital that the panel "will continue aggressive oversight of ActBlue, including additional depositions." All three committees have been responsible for investigating the left-wing fundraising giant. It's not clear how much those depositions will yield, however. The Judiciary Committee revealed through a series of transcripts on Thursday that all 10 ActBlue employees and board members who appeared for closed-door depositions invoked the Fifth Amendment to avoid answering questions. That includes co-founder Matt DeBergalis, whose invocation was first reported by Fox News Digital. ActBlue CEO Regina Wallace-Jones similarly opted to plead the Fifth during a public hearing. The GOP report cited a letter by Wallace-Jones to Steil, which maintained that donations on the platform made by people with addresses outside the U.S. required a passport number for verification. But the Republicans' report alleged that the verification "only ensures that the entered passport number contains a certain number of characters, not that it is a valid U.S. passport number," rendering it an essentially meaningless step. TEXAS AG PAXTON SUES DEM FUNDRAISING PLATFORM ACTBLUE, ALLEGING 'FRAUDULENT AND FOREIGN DONATIONS' The report also included excerpts purporting to show ActBlue supervisors green-lighting donations despite "red flags," including a memo lauding a donation as a "great accept," but noting, "Donor sometimes has an IP in Hong Kong, but none of their other signals raise any eyebrows." Another communication appears to show an ActBlue supervisor maintaining that a denied contribution "should have been accepted." The rest of the memo stated, "It is a foreign contribution, but the name/email match, the IP/billing match, a full address with the correct country code, and there were previously accepted and successful contributions." "The donor uses an Arkansas state code, which isn’t great, but [the] system can be wonky with requiring state codes for foreign donors," the rest of the message stated. ACTBLUE SUES TEXAS AG KEN PAXTON, ALLEGING POLITICAL RETALIATION OVER DEMOCRATS' FUNDRAISING An ActBlue supervisor also allegedly said a contribution "set off a lot of" alarms, but argued the donor should be given the "benefit of the doubt." Yet another appeared to show an ActBlue employee acknowledging that a donor using a Missouri billing address had "all signs point to this person being from Canada," but that X (then Twitter) was used to confirm their identity. But despite the GOP's accusations, the report's evidence also appears to show ActBlue employees standing by the platform. An email from ActBlue employees shows they believe the company to be "the target of bad-faith political attacks at the hands of ill-intentioned operators." ActBlue also previously told the committee "there is no evidence that foreign donations through online or small-dollar contributions are a problem in U.S. elections." The communications excerpts were included in the report and not independently verified by Fox News Digital. It's prompted a firestorm on the right, with House Republicans' campaign arm demanding that Democrats return donations made through ActBlue. "House Democrats cannot claim ignorance while continuing to rely on a fundraising platform facing serious allegations. The [National Republican Congressional Committee] officially calls on every House Democrat to cut ties with ActBlue and return any illegal contributions funneled to their campaigns through the platform," spokesman Mike Marinella said. But when asked if ActBlue would return any donations, the company pointed Fox News Digital back to its statement on the House GOP report. "There’s nothing to see here. After we released findings of a third-party forensic analysis that completely undermined a central claim that they have made against ActBlue, Republicans are refusing to move on," ActBlue said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Instead, they are orchestrating another political stunt before rushing out of town weeks early to go campaign. This coordinated campaign against ActBlue isn’t about the facts, or legislating, it’s about Republicans’ efforts to silence organizations they believe threaten their agenda."

articles.title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico to file lawsuit against Trump's White House ban
articles.summary: The US media outlets say they are defending "the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes".
articles.body:
CNN, Politico and MS NOW have said they will sue the Trump administration after the three US media outlets were barred from the White House.

President Donald Trump announced the ban on Friday, accusing the organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his team. The companies said their reporters were denied access to the building on Saturday.

In a joint statement on Monday, they said they were pursuing legal action to "protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports".

Posting on Truth Social shortly afterwards, Trump said the White House was not "instituting an assault on the Free Press" and he was targeting "FAKE NEWS".

The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.

A statement from CNN, Politico and MS NOW continued: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting.

"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."

BBC News has asked the White House for comment.

Announcing the ban last week, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years".

The US president added that there "may be others to join them".

When later asked by a reporter what he meant by this, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news."

CNN - one of only five US news outlets in the White House press pool for live television - was originally due to cover Trump's trip to the UN General Assembly in New York on Monday and Tuesday.

But the pool slot has remained vacant and instead the staunchly conservative TV outlet, Real America's Voice, was listed as "secondary" crew on the trip.

The pool acts as a representative for the media, sharing material with other outlets to save on finance and space when covering presidential events.

In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.

The same month, the administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.

Trump has been frequently critical of news organisations and his administration has launched legal action against a series of outlets, including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal and the BBC.

Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multimillion dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.

articles.title: Support for press freedom now depends entirely on who is in office
articles.summary: It would be useful right about now if we had an dedicated to sorting fact from fiction. Sadly, no such thing exists in the U.S. today.
articles.body:
When it comes to press freedom, Americans have embraced situational ethics. They support or oppose freedom of the press depending on who holds office, according to Pew Research data released last week .

This evidently went over the Associated Press’s head, however. Its main takeaway was that Democrats are likelier than Republicans to oppose government efforts to curb or censor news reporting.

Republicans were “more likely than Democrats to say the government should be able to require a news story be taken down in cases of national security,” the AP reported , citing Pew. “About 7 in 10 Republicans said this should be allowed, compared to about half of Democrats. A similar gap emerged on the publication of false information.

The story added: “Democrats were [also] more likely than Republicans to prioritize a free press to begin with. About eight in 10 Democrats said a free press is ‘extremely’ or ‘very’ important for society’s well-being, compared to about two-thirds of Republicans.”

Yes, but that claim comes with some caveats. What the AP analysis is missing is the phrase “right now” — as in, Democrats “right now” hold these views.

Because it wasn’t so long ago that the two parties held very different positions, back when a Democrat occupied the White House.

In the first year of the Biden administration, Pew found that the share of Democrats who said the U.S. government should “take steps to restrict false info online, even if it limits” freedom of information, had jumped to 65 percent, up from 40 percent in 2018. The share of Democrats who said tech companies should restrict false information online, even at the expense of free speech, likewise rose from 60 percent to 76 percent during that same period.

In contrast, only 28 percent of Republicans said in 2021 that the government should restrict supposedly false information, down from 37 percent in 2018. Republican support for tech censorship also fell from 48 percent to 37 percent.

July 2023 brought more of the same, only more pronounced.

By then, the share of Democrats who said the government should stamp out “false information” online had risen to 70 percent. The share who said “freedom of information should be protected, even if it means false information can be published” declined to 28 percent, down from 57 percent in 2018.

That same year, 39 percent of Republicans said the government should curb false information online, while 59 percent said freedom of information should be protected even if false information gets published.

Pew put it plainly at the time: “Democrats have become much more supportive than Republicans of the government restricting false information online.”

Then Donald Trump won re-election, and everything changed. By 2025 , the share of Republicans who supported government restrictions on false online information had risen from 39 percent to 43 percent. Meanwhile, the Democratic share had fallen from 70 percent to 58 percent.

The share of Democrats who said freedom of information should be protected even if false information can be published rose from 28 percent to about 40 percent. The Republican share on that count fell slightly, from 59 percent to 55 percent.

By 2026, 64 percent of Democrats said they were “extremely or very concerned about potential restrictions on the freedom of the press in the U.S.,” compared with 29 percent of Republicans. Sixty-one percent of Democrats said they were similarly worried about freedom of speech, compared with 39 percent of Republicans.

The data flatter neither side, though Republican views have swung less wildly from one administration to the next.

What the data show is a split electorate that is sympathetic to freedom of the press and free speech only when such things can advance their political goals. If a free press or free expression should prove troublesome to party aims, then the government should restrict those freedoms.

That’s not principle. That’s just situational ethics.

It would be useful right about now if we had a strictly apolitical institution dedicated to sorting fact from fiction — an institution whose impartial analyses and investigations might cool the otherwise overwhelming urge toward the soft, warm familiarity of tribalism.

Sadly, no such institution exists in the U.S. today. Instead, we have the modern media, which is disliked and distrusted even more than Wall Street , and not without reason.

Becket Adams is a journalist and media critic in Washington.

articles.title: Trump plans ‘AI force’ as pressure for action rises
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ New AI czar to be named ▪ Outlets sue over White House ban ▪ Trump adds security angle to arch ▪ Russia holds wartime elections President Trump is responding to the rising demands to impose guardrails on AI with the creation of an “AI Force,” even as he argues the broader concerns…
articles.body:
President Trump is responding to the rising demands to impose guardrails on AI with the creation of an “AI Force,” even as he argues the broader concerns about the technology running rampant are a “hoax.”

The president announced Saturday that he would launch the body, which he compared to the U.S. Space Force created during his first term, but provided few details about its makeup or responsibilities. He said he would also appoint an AI “czar” to oversee the administration’s handling of the developing technology.

This would be the second person to hold that role in the administration, as venture capitalist David Sacks previously served in the position. He stepped down in March.

“We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows! However, we will also be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System,” Trump said in a Truth Social post .

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessant also laid the groundwork for more global cooperation on AI in talks with his Chinese counterparts in New York on Sunday, NBC News reported . He told reporters that Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping would discuss a mechanism for alerting each other of potential national security issues related to AI, as part of ongoing U.S.-China dialogue on the technology.

Trump has shunned calls for regulation of the industry, despite leaders of the country’s powerful frontier AI firms urging the government to take action. Several current and former AI researchers warned earlier this month that out-of-control AI could result in humanity’s destruction in the next decade or even sooner.

Trump has emphasized that the U.S. cannot lose the AI race with China. He said last week that “guardrails” could be put in place, but a “lot of negative forces” are “bringing up things that won’t happen.”

Even as the president announced his moves on AI this weekend, he continued to push back on the backlash, grouping the “decimation” caused by AI as one of several “hoaxes” created by the Democrats, such as his past impeachments and climate change.

But polling has shown concerns about AI has been a rare unifying issue across the political spectrum. One poll from July showed Americans were nearly three times as likely to be concerned as excited about the potential effects of AI, with Democrats and Republicans providing similar results.

A Politico poll released Wednesday showed almost two-thirds of Americans believe AI poses at least a “moderate” risk of destroying humanity, including a majority of respondents who voted for Trump and a majority who voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024.

Trump seemed to acknowledge the unease with a poll of his followers on Truth Social earlier on Saturday about finding a new name for AI, reasoning that “the words ‘artificial intelligence’ are inaccurate.” He pitched “Superior Intelligence,” “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence” as possible alternatives.

The president’s critics have been eager to pounce on his approach to the technology.

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) cast doubt on the effectiveness of Trump’s AI force during an appearance on CBS News’s “Face the Nation” on Sunday.

“I mean, I don’t know what President Trump’s vision is, I don’t know if he’s using AI in an offensive capability, which would give me a lot of pause,” Khanna said.

The congressman added that an AI agency similar to the Food and Drug Administration needs to be set up.

Former President Obama also slammed Trump’s approach during a Friday interview at Colgate University. He noted Trump’s remark that AI regulations are for “losers.”

“So we’ve got a gap of at least a couple of years where things are moving really fast, and we have an administration that is not capable of or willing to — I would argue both — putting together a serious regulatory framework,” he said.

The focus on AI will be a backdrop of Chinese President Xi Jinping ‘s trip to the U.S. this week, The Hill’s Laura Kelly reports . He’s expected to meet with Trump on Wednesday for the start of his state visit.

Khanna said an “international agreement” must be reached with Xi to have standards including international monitoring and checks through data centers.

“Now, obviously, you can’t just trust the Chinese, but like any agreement, like an arms control agreement, as [former President] Reagan said, you need to trust and verify, and the world has done this before,” he said.
