A federal immigration agent shot and injured a man in Austin, Texas, on Sunday. The man was taken to the hospital in unknown condition.

Trump will meet with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) at the mayor’s house, focusing on issues “affecting New York City and New Yorkers.” The two politicians, despite coming from opposite sides of the spectrum, have enjoyed a cordial relationship while in office.

Trump reversed a decision to launch strikes on Houthi rebels in Yemen on Sunday, just as the military was preparing to begin a wave of attacks at the request of Saudi Arabia, The New York Times reported .

The CNN office at the White House is seen empty following President Trump’s ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Sept. 19, 2026, in Washington.

LOCKOUT : The three media outlets banned from White House grounds on Friday are suing the Trump administration.

“This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,” CNN, MS NOW and Politico said in a joint statement on Monday.

“Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting,” they added. “Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.”

All three outlets said Saturday that their journalists were denied access to the White House and had their credentials confiscated. Trump said he made the decision not because of any specific story or issue but as a “result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS.”

He said additional news outlets could be banned in the future.

The White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA), National Press Club and Knight First Amendment Institute all also denounced the administration’s move.

“The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably,” WHCA President Jacqui Heinrich said in a statement . “That’s why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting.”

▪ The Hill : Wes Moore says Trump uses Constitution as ‘suggestion box.’

▪ Politico : Inside the White House media ban.

NEW ANGLE : Trump said a “top grade military complex” will be part of the triumphal arch bridging Washington, D.C., and Virginia, a change he said was made at the military’s request for “National Security purposes.”

Trump said on Truth Social that the complex will house snipers and drones on the roof and plaza areas.

The announcement comes as the arch, one of the president’s beautification projects in the nation’s capital, is facing a legal challenge from Vietnam War veterans, arguing the administration is seeking to move forward without requisite congressional approval.

The shift from Trump echoes a similar approach that his administration has taken with his White House ballroom project, arguing that it’s necessary for security reasons.

If built, the arch would be 250 feet tall, running along the Arlington Memorial Bridge and across from Arlington National Cemetery.

▪ The Hill : FAA says arch will require ‘eternal flame’ to alert pilots.

▪ ABC News : Trump’s arch construction could run 20 hours a day.

DECISION TIME : Trump is raising the prospect that he could order a major offensive against Iran soon, suggesting “very big things” will happen in the “not-so-distant future.”

Fox News’s Trey Yingst reported that Trump is in a “deciding mode.”

“The president described the current choices on the table as ‘wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal,’” Yingst said. “He added, ‘My question is if and when do I blow the entire nation up? They better behave.’”

Trump previously told Axios that he’s weighing whether to “go in and annihilate” the Iranian regime.

The president has mostly taken an approach of economic pressure in recent weeks to try to force Iranian leaders back to the negotiating table. The eruption of fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi rebels in Yemen has threatened to pull the U.S. into a new front of the war.

Trump is reportedly expected to meet with six Persian Gulf leaders on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly this week. The administration is also allowing a “core delegation” of Iranian officials to attend the session in New York.

▪ The Hill : Kevin Hassett says Trump ‘had to act’ on Iran.

▪ Reuters : U.S., Iran trade threats after Houthi attacks escalate.

CLOSING IN : The Senate is looking to achieve final passage of a major college sports bill that would create national rules for athletes, coaches and the NCAA.

The Protect College Sports Act would enact several provisions to set regulations for the NCAA, including protecting the organization from antitrust lawsuits, establishing caps on revenue sharing and allowing schools to have retention funds for star players.

It would also require agents to register with a state before representing student-athletes, set a five-year window for athletic eligibility, and limit transfers and mid-season coaching moves.

The legislation has yielded opposition from the AFL-CIO, NAACP and the Congressional Black Caucus, but it advanced in the Senate comfortably, 74-24, last week.

As The Hill’s Dominick Mastrangelo reports for Insider , the bill faces an uphill battle in the House when the lower chamber returns after the midterms.

Later, he will meet separately with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and French President Emmanuel Macron at4:10 p.m. and 5:35 p.m., respectively. At 6 p.m., Trump will participate in a Republican National Committee reception followed by a MAGA Inc. dinner.

The House will convene at 10:30 a.m. for a pro forma session.

Elon Musk flashes his T-shirt that reads “DOGE” to the media as he walks on South Lawn of the White House, in Washington, on March 9, 2025.

BUYOUT PUSHBACK : A new round of scrutiny is rising on the defunct Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) following a report that nearly $7 billion was spent for staff to not work.

A Government Accountability Office report estimated that the Trump administration spent $6.7 billion on administrative leave as former DOGE head Elon Musk pushed for widespread buyouts across the federal government.

Employees who accepted a buyout were paid through the end of the fiscal year. Some still received paychecks even though they hadn’t been working for months.

The Hill’s Rebecca Beitsch reports lawmakers from the D.C. area view the report as a referendum on Trump and Musk’s culling of the workforce under the guise of efficiency.

“First of all, how stupid was it to pay people to stay home for four or five months — or longer — getting paid, and they don’t have to do anything, and we’ve robbed the American people of the services they were providing,” said Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), whose district saw 20,000 constituents lose their jobs in the early days of the Trump administration.

The report found salary costs tied to paid leave jumped six times between 2023 and 2025, while the total number of paid administrative leave days rose from 4 million before Trump to 21.6 million last year.

The $6.7 billion spent on buyouts is part of the total $9.5 billion used on paid leave, the report states.

“It was a one-time expense. What did the taxpayer get for it? Using rough averages, the fully loaded cost of a federal employee is about $150,000 per year. For 270,000 employees, that is more than $40 billion in annual costs. These are not one-time costs, but costs incurred every year in perpetuity,” Scott Kupor , the director of the Office of Personnel Management, wrote in a blog post.

But Beitsch reports that critics say the administration isn’t taking other aspects into account, including that 20,000 people were hired to backfill the roles of those who took a buyout. Advocates and lawmakers said these individuals come with less experience.

Russian President Vladimir Putin speaks during a news conference with President Trump at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Alaska, on Aug. 15, 2025.

OCCUPIED ELECTIONS : Over the weekend, Russia began its first legislative elections since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — including in Ukrainian territory that it now occupies.

Voting began on Friday for more than 110 million eligible voters, including in four Ukrainian provinces that Russia has annexed but don’t fully control — Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson. It also held elections in Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014.

Kyiv denounced the elections as illegitimate and called on foreign governments not to recognize the results.

The outcome of the elections was virtually all but certain, as the races featured nominal opposition at best to Russian President Vladimir Putin ‘s party and policies. The Kremlin is hoping to use the elections to demonstrate popular support for the war, stifling dissent to prevent any risks.

The main party, United Russia, was widely expected to maintain its dominant control of the lower house of the Kremlin, the Duma. The only party that openly criticized the war was removed from the ballot.

The elections came as the State Department approved a potential $2.6 billion air defense equipment sale to Ukraine on Friday. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he will meet with Trump at the U.N. General Assembly this week.

Ed Sheeran performs at the 2023 New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival in New Orleans on April 29, 2023.

And finally … Singer Ed Sheeran addressed the controversy surrounding the removal of Macklemore as his opening act over the rapper’s pro-Palestinian comments.

Sheeran said at his Philadelphia concert on Saturday that he has tried not to comment on politics because he wants his music to be about “unity, not division.”

“But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore,” he said.

Sheeran said his heart is “broken by the scale of the devastation” in Gaza, calling the situation “catastrophic and unjustifiable.” He also condemned Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel as “horrific.”

Multiple artists on Sheeran’s tour have left over Macklemore being dropped as the opener. The move came under pressure from New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft and other stadium owners.

articles.title: News outlets banned from White House to sue Trump administration
articles.summary: Officials from CNN, MS NOW and Politico said Monday the media organizations will file a lawsuit against the Trump administration, after their reporters were banned from the White House. “This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government…
articles.body:
Officials from CNN, MS NOW and Politico said Monday the media organizations will file a lawsuit against the Trump administration, after their reporters were banned from the White House.

“This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,” the outlets said in a joint statement.

“Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting,” the statement continued. “Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.”

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

White House officials barred reporters from the outlets from entering White House grounds Saturday, a day after President Trump announced journalists from the organizations would be banned.

Trump cited the outlets’ “constant” reporting of “FAKE NEWS” for the ban.

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” the president wrote Friday on Truth Social.

Trump added that reporters from other outlets could also be banned but did not name specific companies.

The president has held a contentious relationship with reporters dating back to his first term , often accusing them of covering him in a biased manner.

In 2018, the White House revoked the credentials of CNN correspondent Jim Acosta, after he and Trump had a tense back-and-forth during a press conference.

CNN filed suit over the move at the time, before dropping the litigation after the White House lifted Acosta’s suspension.

Jacqui Heinrich, the president of the White House Correspondents Association, called the latest move to bar CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from the White House a violation of the First Amendment.

“The implications extend beyond these organizations: a standard used to exclude one news outlet because of its coverage could be applied to any outlet in the future,” Heinrich, who covers the White House for Fox News, wrote in a statement .

“The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably,” she added.

articles.summary: News outlets CNN, Politico and MS NOW filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration after President Donald Trump banned from covering the White House.
articles.body: Media outlets CNN, Politico and MS NOW plan to file a lawsuit Monday against the Trump administration after President Donald Trump banned them from covering the White House. The president announced the ban Friday on Truth Social, citing what he said was “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” In a joint statement on social media, the three outlets said they notified the administration Monday that they were filing the suit “to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.” “Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting,” the statement continued. “Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.” The White House did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment on the lawsuit. Trump defended his move in a Monday morning Truth Social post, saying the ban was “an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America.” “It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control,” he continued. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” Trump has targeted journalists and outlets he dislikes, but the ban is the most extreme instance so far of the president’s push to hinder press access. Secret Service members turned away reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House grounds and revoked their passes Saturday, prompting backlash from experts and the White House Correspondents’ Association, which called the move unconstitutional. CNN’s and MS NOW’s workspaces in the White House sat empty following their access being withdrawn. The publications have long been part of the White House press pool, a group of media outlets that cover the president. The pool, which is managed by the White House Correspondents’ Association, assigns a small number of reporters each day to cover the president on behalf of the full press corps. The assigned outlet rotates. CNN, now banned, was assigned to pool duty Monday, providing broadcast coverage meant to be shared with all members of the press corps. On Sunday night, the White House sent out its daily media guidance, which did not have any major broadcast outlet included for Monday’s pool duties. Trump has attempted to ban outlets from government spaces before. He barred The Associated Press from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some events after it declined to call the Gulf of Mexico by Trump’s preferred name, the Gulf of America. The AP sued the administration, and the case is ongoing.

articles.title: Beware Beijing bearing gifts as Xi visits America’s dealmaker-in-chief
articles.summary: Access to American markets must come with tough, but fair, questions.
articles.body:
Chinese President Xi Jinping comes to Washington this week, at a time when relations between the U.S. and China are in flux. Beyond the warm handshakes, hugs and polite photos, there are palpable tensions between the world’s two largest economies.

Trade and tariffs are front and center. But no less important is the systematic scrutiny of Chinese firms operating in the U.S. From servers to networking equipment to cooling systems to data centers, Chinese-manufactured components are embedded throughout American digital infrastructure .

More broadly, there is significant Chinese penetration — and in many cases domination — of key American industries, including ports, cars, hospitals, supply chains, rare-earth minerals and the grid itself. This proliferation has accelerated the regulatory reactions of the Department of Defense, Department of Commerce and the Federal Communications Commission, and the imposition of sanctions on several categories of products from China.

Amid this climate, the Trump-Xi Summit still holds promise; the reality is that China and the U.S. need each other more than they care to admit. Even as fierce economic competitors, the world’s two largest economies are conjoined by trade, investment, service and supply chain bonds that are difficult to decouple.

Reports are that Xi will arrive in the U.S. accompanied by a large delegation of Chinese business leaders ready to make deals. In advance, China has been buying substantial amounts of American agricultural products. American farmers surely want to sell more soybeans to China, and other industries are anxious to penetrate the vast Chinese market if allowed.

But the trade imbalance is hard to ignore . Chinese companies have been both successful and savvy in leveraging an open U.S. market to their considerable advantage. Their uncanny ability to meet the needs of the market with affordable, innovative and indispensable products must be admired.

Cheap Chinese drones have helped American farmers to inspect crops and first responders to survey disasters . Chinese telecom equipment offered affordable infrastructure alternatives to U.S. providers. Chinese-made batteries, solar panels and industrial inputs have accelerated new technologies, and popular apps have attracted millions of ordinary American users who just cannot get enough. And inexpensive manufacturing opportunities in China have helped countless American companies, large and small, to lower costs and margins. Suppliers have been less expensive, factories have been more efficient, and technologies have been more innovative

The U.S. did not arrive at this point overnight. Years — in fact, decades — of permissive trade and investment policies by both Democratic and Republican administrations have contributed to the current state of affairs. Remedying, repairing or replacing these policies will take time, but is accelerating under the Trump administration. The shift from enablement to enforcement of new regulations is happening as we speak.

And that brings us to the larger issue of trust.

This administration no longer treats Chinese commercial activity as merely a question of trade. Increasingly, it is viewed through the lenses of security, ownership, control, data, infrastructure and access.

The FCC’s covered list , created pursuant to federal law, identifies communications equipment and services deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to national security or the security and safety of Americans. Huawei, ZTE, Hytera, Hikvision and Dahua have long appeared on it. More recently, the list has expanded to cover categories of foreign-produced drones and certain foreign-produced routers. The FCC also has adopted rules restricting authorization, marketing and importation of covered equipment.

The Pentagon operates under a different statute and for a different purpose. Its Section 1260H list identifies companies that the Department of Defense determines are Chinese military companies operating directly or indirectly in the United States. The government describes the list as part of its effort to address China’s military-civil fusion strategy, through which ostensibly civilian technology and commercial capabilities may contribute to military modernization.

The Commerce Department maintains yet another regime. Its Entity List restricts exports, reexports and transfers involving designated entities. In 2025, Commerce expanded those restrictions to reach certain affiliates owned 50 percent or more by listed companies. In other words, Washington has moved beyond looking merely at the name on the door — ownership matters too.

Then there is the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States , export controls, outbound investment restrictions and Treasury sanctions . These programs are not interchangeable, and being placed on one government list does not necessarily mean that a company is “sanctioned.” The legal consequences differ considerably. But together they reveal something larger.

The era of automatic access is over, which may be the most important message for the Chinese business leaders accompanying Xi on his visit.

America remains one of the most attractive markets in the world, with deep capital markets, sophisticated consumers, world-class research institutions, enormous purchasing power and a legal system that gives foreign companies significant rights and protections. CFIUS itself describes its mission as protecting national security while preserving America’s attractiveness to foreign investment. But access to American markets must come with tough, but fair, questions.

Who owns the company? Who ultimately controls it? Where does the data go? What relationship does the company have with the Chinese government or military? Can American regulators obtain truthful information about its operations? And perhaps most important, would an American company receive comparable treatment in China?

If these basic questions cannot be answered on a company-by-company basis, to the satisfaction of U.S. law and American officials, it does not matter how good the deals are that Chinese business leaders come to propose. The Chinese must ensure that they will abide by a few fundamental principles: namely, transparency, reciprocity, security, standards and compliance.

None of this requires the U.S. and China to stop doing business together. Nor does it erase the benefits that Chinese goods, investment and manufacturing have brought to American consumers and companies. But it does mean that the relationship has indelibly changed and is in the process of being rebalanced. And that is good for both nations.

Adonis Hoffman served in senior legal roles at the Federal Communications Commission and in the U.S. House of Representatives, where he was counsel to the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

articles.title: US strikes on alleged drug boats could be crimes against humanity, says UN
articles.summary: A report says the attacks, of which there have been at least 68, were not self-defence.
articles.body:
A UN report has concluded that recent US airstrikes on vessels allegedly trafficking drugs breached international law and could constitute crimes against humanity.

The report by Special Rapporteur Ben Saul said since September last year there had been at least 68 US strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific, outside US territorial waters, which killed more than 220 people.

Saul said that even if targets could be identified as members of designated terrorist groups, they had not staged an armed attack on the US which would trigger a right to self-defence under international law.

The report comes two days after the US military said it killed four people in a strike on a vessel in the Caribbean.

"Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists," Southcom, which commands US forces in the region, said in a statement about the latest attack, which was accompanied by a grainy video.

But in a briefing note released by the UN Human Rights Council on Monday, Saul said that "such attacks amount to serial extrajudicial killings in violation of the right to life, being unjustified in national or personal self-defence or under international humanitarian law, the international law of the sea, narcotics suppression conventions, or international counter-terrorism law".

"There are reasonable grounds to believe that the reported 68 attacks that killed 223 people constituted crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law," Saul concluded.

BBC News has contacted the White House and State Department for a response to the report.

Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has previously said the overall operation is aimed at removing "narco-terrorists from our hemisphere" and securing the US from "the drugs that are killing our people".

The US military launched the operation, known as "Southern Spear", in early September.

However, officials have not offered definitive evidence that the vessels targeted are involved in trafficking.

Since the beginning, experts have questioned the legality of the strikes, which initially drew strong criticism from Latin American leaders whose citizens have been targeted.

However, Nicolás Maduro, who was the Venezuelan leader at the time and opposed the strikes, was seized by US forces in a dramatic and highly controversial night-time raid on the capital Caracas at the beginning of this year.

Another outspoken critic of Operation Southern Spear, Colombia's left-wing president at the time, Gustavo Petro, stood down in August after a Trump-backed candidate won June's presidential election.

articles.title: Party division is at its peak, but the extremes have never been closer to each other
articles.summary: Originally dubbed the “Horseshoe theory,” the concept argues that at the extremes, the political left and right eventually bend towards each other.
articles.body:
On the surface, Democrats and Republicans are further apart today than perhaps at any point in American history. According to Pew Research , 80 percent of Americans believe that Republican and Democratic voters “cannot agree on plans, policies, or basic facts.”

In a deeper sense however, the growing political divide obscures something more consequential: the loudest voices on the far left and far right increasingly sound alike. Originally dubbed the “ Horseshoe theory ,” the concept argues that at the extremes, the political left and right eventually bend towards each other.

Writing in the Wall Street Journal , Greg Ip named this coalition the “Horseshoe Party.” As he sees it, leading this hypothetical party are Vice President JD Vance on the populist right and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on the socialist left. The two agree on almost nothing, except for a deep suspicion of free markets, elites and the idea that government should stay out of markets.

Unfortunately, the convergence extends well beyond Ip’s theoretical party.

President Trump has directed the government to take stakes in private companies, a position traditionally anathema to Republicans. Last year, Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) joined to co-sponsor a bill aimed at capping credit card interest rates — a policy originating with Trump. The House’s companion bill was introduced by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.), who authored a children’s book suggesting former President Biden stole the 2020 election and refers to herself as a “pro-life extremist.”

Likewise, Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) have teamed up to raise taxes on high earners. And this month, Sanders and Steve Bannon co-headlined a conference calling for limits on artificial intelligence.

This convergence isn’t limited to politicians. Tucker Carlson — long one of the most influential conservative voices — has backed Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for Senate in Michigan over the Trump-backed Republican.

Yet perhaps nowhere is this convergence more prevalent than on foreign policy, particularly Israel. The Iran war may have fractured the MAGA base — Carlson has said Trump should be removed from office — but on Israel, one would find it impossible to discern whether a criticism was voiced by Carlson, Candace Owens, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Green (R-Ga.), or Reps. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich), Ocasio-Cortez, Ro Khanna (D-Calif) or extreme left-wing commentator Hasan Piker.

These camps are not united in pursuit of an overarching political direction — they agree on what they are against far more than what they are for. Instead, they’re tied together by anger towards common enemies: elites, foreign countries and big corporations which they feel have rigged the system. Trump’s own rise is both a symptom and a result of this sentiment.

As one well-known policy analyst wrote , “Trump has re-educated, or mis-educated a lot of Republican voters into thinking everything is rigged. It’s how Bernie Sanders thinks about the economy.”

Both parties’ establishments bear some responsibility. The bipartisan center presided over a period of globalization that devastated American communities, wars that cost tremendous blood and treasure and an economy whose gains too often failed to reach working families. It was also too slow to change course when voters demanded it.

Acknowledging these failures does not make the Horseshoe Party’s policies any less dangerous. Capping interest rates would choke off credit working families depend on. Abandoning Israel would not make America richer or safer. And stopping AI development, rather than regulating it responsibly, would cede leadership of this critical technology to China.

To be sure, political realignments do periodically occur, and neither extreme currently commands a majority. Pew’s Political typology finds that the most progressive bloc makes up just 7 percent of the electorate, while its counterpart on the right ranges between 9 and 12 percent.

However, as both parties increasingly abandon the center, candidates run to their most vocal, most extreme, base. As a result, candidates whose statements or policies would have been disqualifying a decade ago become nominees, taking these views into the mainstream.

That brings us to 2028. The energy is at the poles, but the votes that decide presidential elections remain in the center, for now. Whoever captures that with genuine solutions to the legitimate grievances that first pushed Americans to the extremes should have the votes when it matters.

Put another way, a candidate who promises restraint abroad without retreat or abandoning allies or offers a solution to the affordability crisis without price controls or government-run grocery stores will be stronger than simply the most populist one.

Right now, however, neither party has that candidate. Vance bet his future on being heir to Trump’s populism and expanding it. For Democrats, former Vice President Kamala Harris and California Gov. Gavin Newsom attempt to present as pragmatic but often concede the debate to the progressive wing.

Ultimately, the extremes converged because the old center failed. American jobs were shipped overseas, national debt ballooned and paychecks seemingly buy less every month.

If moderate Democrats or Republicans fail to reclaim the center by offering credible solutions — without the establishment’s complacency or the populists’ rage — voters will continue being pulled to the extremes, and our country will be significantly worse off.

Douglas E. Schoen and Carly Cooperman are pollsters and partners with the public opinion company Schoen Cooperman Research based in New York. They are co-authors of the book “ America: Unite or Die. ”

articles.title: Trump denies ‘instituting an assault on the free press’
articles.summary: President Trump on Monday denied he is “instituting an assault” on the press after three outlets he recently banned from covering the White House announced plans to sue the administration over the move. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, arguing…
articles.body:
President Trump on Monday denied he is “instituting an assault” on the press after three outlets he recently banned from covering the White House announced plans to sue the administration over the move.

“The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” Trump wrote on Truth Social , arguing that it is instead “instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS.”

“It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” he continued.

The defense comes days after the president barred CNN, MSNOW, and Politico from the White House over their coverage, which he argued lacked credibility. The outlets threatened legal action in response.

“This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,” the companies said in a joint statement.

“Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting,” the statement continued. “Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.”

On Saturday, journalists from the three outlets were denied entry to White House grounds and had their passes confiscated.

The ban has drawn backlash from both sides of the aisle, with critics arguing it constitutes a violation of the First Amendment.
